name: Leo
introduction: is the Lion, one of the few constellations that truly resembles its namesake: a crouching lion whose head and mane form a backward question mark called the Sickle. In Greek myth, it is the Nemean lion slain by Hercules. It is a zodiac constellation, best seen on northern spring evenings.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: [Regulus](hip:49669), the lion’s heart, lies almost exactly on the ecliptic, so the Moon and planets often pass close to it, and the Moon regularly hides it. Regulus spins so fast, once every 16 hours, that it is flattened into an egg shape; a little faster, and it would fly apart. A faint white dwarf companion orbits it closely.

Every November, the Leonid meteors, debris from Comet Tempel–Tuttle, radiate from the Sickle. In 1833, a Leonid storm produced tens of thousands of meteors per hour and launched the scientific study of meteors.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Algieba](hip:50583), in the mane, is a beautiful pair of golden giants, one of which has a planet. [Denebola](hip:57632), the lion’s tail, is a white star 36 light-years away with a dusty debris disk. [Zosma](hip:54872) and [Chertan](hip:54879) mark the lion’s back and hip.
One of the Sun’s nearest neighbors, the faint red dwarf [Wolf 359](id:wolf-359), lies in Leo, only 7.9 light-years away. [AD Leonis](id:10pc-0102) is a nearby flare star known for powerful outbursts.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Beneath the lion’s body lies the Leo Triplet, M65, M66 and NGC 3628, three spiral galaxies close enough to see together in a small telescope. M95, M96 and M105 form another group, and the faint Leo I dwarf galaxy hides in Regulus’s glare. The pulsar [PSR J0953+0755](id:psr-j0953p0755) is one of the nearest known, spinning almost four times a second.
